question: What pressure change in the chest cavity allows air to move into the lungs when you breathe in?

options.C: Intrapleural pressure rises above atmospheric pressure
options.D: Intrapleural pressure drops below atmospheric pressure

explanation: When the breathing muscles expand the chest wall, it creates a lower pressure area inside that pulls air inward. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h1)

question: How does oxygen move from the air sacs into the bloodstream?

options.A: Facilitated transport via specialized carrier proteins
options.C: Osmosis driven by plasma protein concentration
options.D: Simple diffusion along a pressure gradient

explanation: Gases move naturally from an area of higher pressure in the air sacs to a lower pressure in the capillary blood. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h1)

question: What is the main problem in obstructive lung disorders?

options.B: Thickened alveolar walls preventing simple diffusion
options.C: Reduced total lung capacity limiting full expansion
options.D: Increased airway resistance limiting rapid exhalation

explanation: Obstructive conditions trap air inside the lungs because narrowed airways make it hard to push air out quickly. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h2)

question: A patient has a stiff chest wall and reduced lung volumes. What type of breathing defect is this?
explanation: Stiffness of the chest wall limits lung expansion, which is the key sign of a restrictive lung disorder. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h2)

question: A blood clot in the lungs stops blood flow to ventilated air sacs. What is this mismatch called?
explanation: When breathing continues without blood supply, the affected area acts as physiological dead space where no gas exchange happens. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h3)

question: What happens to the ventilation-perfusion ratio when an air sac fills with fluid and gets no air?

options.A: It fluctuates randomly based on cardiac output
options.B: It remains at the normal baseline of 0.8
options.C: It drops to zero, creating a true shunt
options.D: It rises significantly, creating dead space

explanation: When an air sac has blood flow but no air, it is a shunt where deoxygenated blood bypasses gas exchange. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h3)

question: Which change is typical in emphysema?

options.A: Destruction of alveolar walls and loss of lung elasticity
options.B: Hypertrophy of submucosal glands with excessive sputum production
options.C: Fibrotic scarring of the pleural space
options.D: Reversible smooth muscle bronchospasm triggered by allergens

explanation: Emphysema breaks down the elastic walls of air sacs, destroying the surface area needed for gas exchange and trapping air. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why do people with chronic bronchitis get frequent chest infections?

options.A: Decreased pulmonary blood flow starves white blood cells of oxygen
options.B: Impaired ciliary function prevents effective clearance of mucus and bacteria
options.C: Destruction of alveolar macrophages stops phagocytosis entirely
options.D: Permanent dilation of alveoli creates pools of stagnant fluid

explanation: Damaged tiny hairs in the airways cannot sweep out heavy mucus, allowing bacteria to grow easily. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h4)

question: How does pulmonary fibrosis make gas exchange difficult?

options.A: Scar tissue thickens the alveolar-capillary membrane, slowing diffusion
options.B: Destruction of pulmonary capillaries creates high dead space
options.C: Mucus plugs block the main bronchi, preventing airflow
options.D: Loss of surfactant causes widespread alveolar collapse

explanation: Extra scar tissue widens the distance that oxygen and carbon dioxide must travel to cross into the capillaries. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h5)

question: Which condition is an outside (extrinsic) cause of restrictive lung disease?
explanation: Spinal deformities restrict the movement of the chest wall and rib cage rather than damaging the lung tissue inside. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h5)

question: What causes blood vessels in the lungs to tighten up when someone has long-term low oxygen?

options.A: Destruction of heart valves reducing cardiac output
options.B: Low alveolar oxygen tension constricting local arterioles
options.C: High systemic blood pressure backing up into the lungs
options.D: Excess carbon dioxide dissolving in the pulmonary veins

explanation: Low oxygen in the air sacs causes small blood vessels nearby to squeeze shut, routing blood to better-aired areas but raising pressure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h6)

question: What is the term for right-sided heart failure caused by lung disease?
explanation: Cor pulmonale specifically means the right side of the heart enlarges and fails because of long-term pressure from lung problems. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h6)

question: How do the kidneys respond when the body has low oxygen levels for a long time?

options.A: Retention of hydrogen ions to normalize blood pH
options.B: Excretion of excess bicarbonate via concentrated urine
options.C: Release of erythropoietin to stimulate red blood cell production
options.D: Secretion of renin to raise systemic blood pressure

explanation: Low blood oxygen tells the kidneys to release erythropoietin, which signals the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h7)

question: Why can turning blue (cyanosis) be a late and sometimes missed sign of low oxygen?

options.A: Peripheral vessels constrict too quickly to show skin color changes
options.B: Anemic patients have enough hemoglobin to prevent color change
options.C: Carbon dioxide levels always mask the blue skin discoloration
options.D: It requires a high absolute amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin to be visible

explanation: Patients with severe anemia may have dangerously low oxygen levels without looking blue because they do not have enough hemoglobin to show the color change. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h7)
